'''''Abutilon theophrasti''','' also known as '''velvetleaf''', '''velvet plant''', '''velvetweed''' and the '''Chinese jute''',<ref>"velvetweed" in ''The Columbia-Viking Desk Encyclopedia'' (1953), New York:  Viking.</ref> is an [[annual plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Malvaceae]] that is native to [[Central Asia|Central]] and [[East Asia]]. It is the [[type species]] of the [[genus]] ''[[Abutilon]]''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Abutilon|url= https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110810104311611|work=Oxford Reference}}</ref> Its [[botanical name|specific epithet]], ''theophrasti,'' commemorates the ancient Greek botanist-philosopher [[Theophrastus]].<ref>{{cite web|last=De Ruff|first=Robert|title=A short description of ''Abutilon theophrasti''|url=http://nathistoc.bio.uci.edu/Plants%20of%20Upper%20Newport%20Bay%20(Robert%20De%20Ruff)/Malvaceae/Abutilon%20theophrasti.htm|work=Plants of Upper Newport Bay}}</ref>

==Description==
Velvetleaf grows 3–8 feet tall on branched, stout stems covered in downy hairs. The annual plant grows during the warmer seasons, germinating in the spring and flowering in the summer. Velvetleaf's leaves are large and heart-shaped with pointed tips at their ends, which grow alternately at different points along the length of the stem. The leaves are attached to thick, long stems, and when crushed, release an odor.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web|url=https://www.kingcounty.gov/services/environment/animals-and-plants/noxious-weeds/weed-identification/velvetleaf.aspx|title=Velvetleaf Identification and Control Abutilon theophrasti|date=18 September 2018|website=KingCounty}}</ref>

The plant's flowers are yellow and grow up to an inch in diameter, with five petals attached at the base. Flowers grow on stalks and can either be found in clusters or individually where the stalk meets the leaf stem.<ref name=":02"/>

Pod-like capsules produced by the plant consist of 12-15 wood segments that form cup-like rings. Through the maturation of the seeds, the segments remain joined, and upon maturation, the mature seeds are released through vertical slits on the outside of the capsule.<ref name=":02"/>

== Biology ==

=== Reproduction ===
During reproduction, the plant generates a number of seeds ranging between 700 and 44,200 units per plant. The seeds take 17–22 days to mature once pollinated. Seeds can last for about 50 years when stored in a dry location or in the soil. In order to disperse the seeds for reproduction, each [[Gynoecium|carpel]] in the plant is opened with a vertical slit along the outer edge. For successful germination of the seeds, the temperature must range between 24 and 30 °C.<ref name="Abutilon theophrasti velvet leaf">{{Cite journal|last1=Rojas-Sandoval |first1=Julissa |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/1987|title=Abutilon theophrasti (velvet leaf)|website=www.cabi.org|date=2022 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.1987 |language=en|access-date=11 February 2019|doi-access=free}}</ref> Velvet plants are able to grow in various types of soil, from gray-brown [[podzol]]s and sandy to clay [[loam]]s with an ideal [[Soil pH|soil pH range]] between 6.1 and 7.8, depending on location.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Canadian Science Publishing|journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science|doi=10.4141/cjps88-127|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Cultivation and medicinal uses==
Velvetleaf has been grown in [[China]] since around 2000 BCE for its strong, [[jute]]-like [[bast fibre]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Velvetleaf (Abutilon theophrasti) |url=https://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/weeds/plants/velvetleaf.htm |website=www.illinoiswildflowers.info}}</ref> The plant is known as ''maabulha'' in the [[Maldives]] and its leaves were part of the traditional [[Maldivian cuisine]], usually finely chopped and mixed with [[Maldives fish]] and grated [[coconut]] in a dish known as ''[[mas huni]]''.<ref name="ReferenceA">[[Xavier Romero-Frias]], ''The Maldive Islanders, A Study of the Popular Culture of an Ancient Ocean Kingdom'', Barcelona 1999, {{ISBN|84-7254-801-5}}</ref> The seeds are eaten in China and [[Kashmir]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nwcb.wa.gov/weed_info/Written_findings/Abutilon_theophrasti.html |title=Velvetleaf |publisher=Written Findings of the State Noxious Weed Control Board - Class A Weed |date=February 2000 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060616045241/http://www.nwcb.wa.gov/weed_info/Written_findings/Abutilon_theophrasti.html |archive-date=16 June 2006 }}</ref> The plant is also used to make ropes, coarse cloth, nets, paper, and caulk for boats, and is still cultivated in China to this day.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://extension.tennessee.edu/publications/Documents/W167.pdf|title=Velvetleaf|last=Steckel|first=Larry|date=July 2007|website=The University of Tennessee}}</ref> Velvetleaf is used in [[Chinese traditional medicine]] as a treatment for dysentery and to treat eye injuries, including opacity of the cornea.<ref name=":0" /> The leaves of the velvet leaf contain 0.01% of rutin and are used for a soothing, lubricant treatment that softens irritated tissues. When the leaves are softened, they can be used as a remedy for ulcers. The bark of velvetleaf can reduce the flow of bodily fluids such as blood, secretions, and mucus, and promote the flow of urine.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Abutilon+theophrasti|title=Abutilon theophrasti China Jute, Velvetleaf, Butterprint Buttonweed Jute, China Mallow, Indian Velvet Leaf PFAF Plant Database|website=pfaf.org|access-date=11 February 2019}}</ref>

==Invasive species==
In the [[midwestern United States|midwestern]] and [[northeastern United States|northeastern]] regions of the US, eastern [[Canada]], and the [[Eastern Mediterranean]], ''A. theophrasti'' is considered a damaging weed to agricultural crops, especially [[Maize|corn]] and [[soybean]]s.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.css.cornell.edu/WeedEco/Published%20Seed%20Sci%20Res.%2011%20335-343.pdf |author=Hameed A. Baloch, Antonio DiTommaso and Alan K. Watson |title=Intrapopulation variation in ''Abutilon theophrasti'' seed mass and its relationship to seed germinability |publisher=Seed Science Research (2001) 11, 335–343 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100628165531/http://www.css.cornell.edu/weedeco/Published%20Seed%20Sci%20Res.%2011%20335-343.pdf |archive-date=28 June 2010 }}</ref> It is also listed as an unwanted organism in New Zealand and in several countries in Europe and by the EU, especially in Central Europe due to its invasive nature.<ref>{{cite web |date=3 May 2024 |title=Velvetleaf weed management | NZ Government |url=https://www.mpi.govt.nz/biosecurity/exotic-pests-and-diseases-in-new-zealand/long-term-biosecurity-management-programmes/velvetleaf/#report |website=www.mpi.govt.nz}}</ref><ref>https://alien.jrc.ec.europa.eu/spexplorer/species/factsheetprintpreview?speciesId=R00033</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Follak |first=Swen |last2=Aldrian |first2=Ulrike |last3=Schwarz |first3=Michael |date=2014 |title=Spread Dynamics of Abutilon theophrasti in Central Europe |url=https://www.agriculturejournals.cz/pdfs/pps/2014/03/07.pdf |journal=Plant Protect. Sci. |volume=50 |issue=3 |pages=157-163}}</ref>

Since being introduced to [[North America]] in the 18th century, velvetleaf has become an [[invasive species]] in agricultural regions of the eastern and midwestern United States. It is one of the most detrimental weeds to [[Maize|corn]], causing decreases of up to 34% of crop yield if not controlled and costing hundreds of millions of dollars per year in control and damage. Velvetleaf is an extremely competitive plant, so much so that it can steal nutrients and water from crops.<ref>Davis, K. Renner, C. Sprague, L. Dyer, D. Mutch (2005). Integrated Weed Management. MSU</ref> Because of the season it germinates in, the plant matures right before the fall harvest on farms.{{Citation needed|date=February 2024}}

Velvetleaf is a tall plant that can cause the shorter crops around it to not thrive by severely reducing light penetration into them. Not only does it affect crop plants by starving them of light, but it also houses different diseases and pests of crops like corn, cotton, soybeans, and others. Examples of pests and diseases that velvetleaf harbors are maize pests, tobacco pests, and soybean diseases.{{Citation needed|date=February 2024}}

When destroyed, the plant releases a chemical odor that is also known to be harmful to surrounding crops when released into the soil by inhibiting the germination of crop seeds.<ref name=":02"/> In order to eradicate velvetleaf, individual plants should be dug up or pulled out manually and not tilled or plowed to avoid seed germination. The plant can also be mowed while it is still small.<ref name=":02" /> 

Velvetleaf can be controlled by herbicides. As an early emerging weed, farmer, care needs to be taken when applying post-emergence herbicides, to avoid waiting until after plants have exceeded the maximum post-emergence height.<ref>https://www.canr.msu.edu/weeds/extension/velvetleaf</ref> Additional methods of control include crop rotation and delaying fall tillage to prevent seeds from entering the seed bank.<ref name="cornell">https://blogs.cornell.edu/weedid/velvetleaf/</ref>

This species is typically found in areas where the soil has been disturbed. This causes the dormant seeds in the soil, which can persist for up to fifty years,<ref name="cornell"></ref> to be brought closer to the surface, allowing for growth when the soil is at an optimally warm temperature.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wimastergardener.org/article/velvetleaf-abutilon-theophrasti/|title=Velvetleaf, Abutilon theophrasti|website=Master Gardener Program|language=en-US|access-date=11 February 2019|archive-date=12 February 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190212011324/https://wimastergardener.org/article/velvetleaf-abutilon-theophrasti/|url-status=dead}}</ref>
